catalog_quote: Wurm 1975:493-494: "A few notes may be added here on Fasu (Loeweke and May 1965, 1966, Franklin and Voorhoeve 1973) and Foe (J. Rule 1952, W. M. Rule 1965, Franklin and Voorhoeve 1973) as representatives of the two families. ... 2.7.3.5.3. Foe (East Kutubu Family). Phonology. Consonants: t k ʔ / b d g / f s h / v / m n / r / w y. Vowels: i u / e o / a. Phonemic nasalisation is present. Suprasegmentals: A two-tone system is present." -- Weiner 1988:xvii-xviii: "The Foi language was first analyzed by the linguist-missionary Murray Rule. Along with his wife Joan Rule, he produced an unpublished grammar and dictionary of Foi during their stay at the Asia Pacific Christian Mission station at Inu, Lake Kutubu. I thus employ Rule's orthography (1977:8-10). ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Foe is reported to have phonemic vowel nasalisation and a two-way (high/low) lexical tone contrast of low functional load (a small number of minimal pairs); none of the accessible sources says anything about the position or existence of word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Weiner: tone contrast 'affect[s] only a small number of word pairs'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tonemes on lexical items; no statement about stress domain, citation forms or phrase prosody. Both statements are second-hand summaries resting on Rule's descriptions (J. Rule 1952; W. M. Rule 1965/1977:8-10).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to Foe/Foi of Lake Kutubu and the Mubi valley (glottocode foii1241; Weiner's fieldwork was among the Upper Mubi Foi at Hegeso, Rule's at Inu on Lake Kutubu, i.e. the Kutubu [kutu1266] and Mubi [mubi1239] dialects). Weiner notes only 'minor dialectical differences' among the three Foi populations.

tone_statements.quote: (d) TONE. Tone is also present in the language, with a change of key or tone on the same word making a change in the meaning. Fortunately there are only two tone patterns, and these are superimposed over the whole word. These two patterns are: 1. a lower tone on each of the syllables, with the final syllable going to a high tone & then falling down to low if it is the final word in the sentence. 2. a high tone on each syllable of the word, dropping down on the final syllable if that word is the last in a clause [...] It is therefore clear that tone & stress have to be taken together as a unit.
